nodes.title: Origin of Magnetism & Atomic Dipole Moments
points: Magnetism in materials originates from atomic electron motion: (1) Orbital motion around the nucleus, (2) Spin motion about its own axis, (3) Nuclear spin (very small, negligible).
Total magnetic dipole moment of an atom is the vector sum of orbital and spin magnetic dipole moments: M_net = M_orbital + M_spin.
In paired electrons, magnetic moments cancel out due to opposite spins (basis of diamagnetism).
In atoms with unpaired electrons, net permanent magnetic dipole moment exists (basis of paramagnetism and ferromagnetism).

nodes.title: Magnetization, Magnetic Intensity & Permeability
points: Magnetization M_z (or M): Net magnetic dipole moment per unit volume of the material: M_z = M_net / V. SI unit: A/m. Dimensions: [M⁰L⁻¹T⁰I¹].
Magnetic Intensity (H): External magnetizing field: H = B₀ / μ₀. SI unit: A/m. Dimensions: [M⁰L⁻¹T⁰I¹] (same unit as Magnetization).
Total Magnetic Induction inside a material: B = μ₀ (H + M_z) = μ H.
Magnetic Susceptibility χ_m: Ratio of magnetization to magnetic intensity: χ_m = M_z / H (dimensionless scalar).
Relative Permeability μ_r: μ_r = μ / μ₀ = 1 + χ_m.

nodes.title: Diamagnetism & Properties of Diamagnetic Materials
points: Origin: Paired electrons; net atomic dipole moment is zero. External magnetic field induces an opposing dipole moment according to Lenz's law.
Key Properties: (1) Weakly repelled by magnets; (2) Move from stronger to weaker parts of a non-uniform magnetic field; (3) A thin rod suspended in uniform field aligns PERPENDICULAR to field lines.
Susceptibility: χ_m is small, negative (−10⁻⁵ to −10⁻⁹), and INDEPENDENT of temperature.
Relative permeability: μ_r is slightly less than 1 (0 ≤ μ_r < 1).
Examples: Bismuth (most diamagnetic), Copper, Lead, Gold, Water, Nitrogen, Diamond.
Superconductors & Meissner Effect: Superconductors expel magnetic fields completely (B_inside = 0 ⟹ χ_m = −1, μ_r = 0, perfect diamagnetism).

nodes.title: Paramagnetism & Curie's Law
points: Origin: Unpaired electrons; each atom has a permanent magnetic dipole moment, but thermal agitation keeps them randomly oriented in zero external field (net M = 0).
Key Properties: (1) Weakly attracted by magnets; (2) Move from weaker to stronger parts of a non-uniform field; (3) Suspended rod aligns PARALLEL to magnetic field lines.
Susceptibility: χ_m is small and positive (+10⁻³ to +10⁻⁵).
Relative permeability: μ_r is slightly greater than 1 (μ_r > 1).
Curie's Law: Magnetic susceptibility of paramagnetic substances is inversely proportional to absolute temperature: χ_m = C / T, where C is Curie's constant.
Saturation magnetization occurs at very low temperatures and very high magnetic fields.
Examples: Aluminium, Platinum, Chromium, Manganese, Oxygen gas, Liquid oxygen.

nodes.title: Ferromagnetism & Domain Theory
points: Origin: Unpaired electrons with strong quantum mechanical exchange interaction aligning atomic dipoles spontaneously into microscopic regions called Domains (~10¹¹ to 10¹⁵ atoms).
Within each domain, all atomic dipoles are parallel and saturated. In an unmagnetized substance, domains are randomly oriented, giving zero net magnetization.
Magnetization Process: (1) Weak external field causes domain wall displacement (favourably oriented domains expand); (2) Strong external field causes domain rotation into field direction.
Key Properties: (1) Strongly attracted by magnets; (2) Move rapidly from weaker to stronger parts of non-uniform field; (3) Strongly align parallel to field lines.
Susceptibility and Permeability: χ_m ≫ 1 (very large, positive, ~10³ to 10⁵); μ_r ≫ 1.
Examples: Iron (Fe), Cobalt (Co), Nickel (Ni), Gadolinium (Gd), Alnico.

nodes.title: Curie Temperature & Curie-Weiss Law
points: Curie Temperature (T_c): The critical temperature above which a ferromagnetic material loses its spontaneous domain magnetization and transforms into a paramagnetic material.
Curie Temperature values: Iron T_c ≈ 1043 K (770 °C); Cobalt T_c ≈ 1394 K; Nickel T_c ≈ 631 K (358 °C).
Curie-Weiss Law (for T > T_c): Susceptibility in paramagnetic phase above T_c: χ_m = C / (T − T_c).
Thermal agitation above T_c breaks domain exchange coupling, randomizing atomic dipole orientations.

nodes.title: Magnetic Hysteresis Loop (B–H Curve)
points: Hysteresis: Phenomenon of lagging of magnetic induction B (or magnetization M) behind magnetizing intensity H in a ferromagnetic substance during a cycle of magnetization.
Retentivity (Remanence / Residual Magnetism): The magnetic induction B remaining in the specimen when external magnetizing field H is reduced to zero.
Coercivity: The magnitude of reverse magnetizing field H required to completely demagnetize the material (reduce B to zero).
Hysteresis Loss: The area enclosed by the B–H hysteresis loop represents the energy lost per unit volume per cycle as heat in the core.
Work done per cycle per unit volume: W = ∮ B dH.

formulas.label: Hysteresis energy loss
formulas.expr: Energy Loss / (Volume × Cycle) = Area of B–H loop

nodes.title: Permanent Magnets vs Electromagnets
points: Permanent Magnets (e.g., Steel, Alnico, Ticonal): Require high retentivity (to retain magnetism), high coercivity (so stray fields do not demagnetize it), and large hysteresis loop.

Electromagnets & Transformer Cores (e.g., Soft Iron): Require high retentivity, LOW coercivity (easily demagnetized), high permeability μ_r (large field with small current), and narrow hysteresis loop (low energy loss).
Magnetic Shielding: A high-permeability ferromagnetic material (like soft iron) redirects magnetic field lines through itself, shielding the inner enclosed space from external magnetic fields.

formulas.label: Soft iron properties
formulas.expr: High μ_r , Low Coercivity , Narrow B-H Loop

formulas.label: Steel/Alnico properties
formulas.expr: High Retentivity , High Coercivity , Broad B-H Loop

nodes.title: Must-Know Board Topics & Comparison Table
points: Board Favourite #1: Explain origin of ferromagnetism on the basis of Domain Theory.

Board Favourite #2: Compare Diamagnetic, Paramagnetic, and Ferromagnetic substances on the basis of: (1) Origin, (2) Behaviour in non-uniform field, (3) Susceptibility χ, (4) Permeability μ_r, (5) Temperature dependence.
Board Favourite #3: Define and explain the terms: (1) Magnetization, (2) Magnetic intensity, (3) Magnetic susceptibility, (4) Retentivity, (5) Coercivity.
Board Favourite #4: Draw and label B–H hysteresis curve and explain hysteresis loss.
Board Favourite #5: State Curie's law and Curie-Weiss law with temperature graphs.

nodes.title: MHT-CET Shortcuts, Meissner Effect & Unit Traps
points: Identical Units Trap: Magnetization M and Magnetic Intensity H have the EXACT SAME unit: A/m (or A·m⁻¹). Dimensions: [M⁰L⁻¹T⁰I¹].
Susceptibility Trap: Magnetic susceptibility χ_m is a DIMENSIONLESS quantity (pure number).
Meissner Effect Shortcut: Superconductor has B = 0 inside, χ_m = −1, μ_r = 0 (perfect diamagnet).
Temperature Dependency Trap: Diamagnetic susceptibility χ_dia is completely independent of temperature. Paramagnetic follows χ ∝ 1/T. Ferromagnetic follows χ ∝ 1/(T − T_c).
Soft Iron vs Steel Trap: Soft iron has higher retentivity than steel, but steel has much higher coercivity. Hence, soft iron makes better electromagnets; steel makes better permanent magnets.
Liquid / Gas Behaviour: Diamagnetic liquid in U-tube depresses in magnetic field; paramagnetic liquid rises.
